answer.label: Not Mark Twain — coined by Arthur G. Lewis in 1911
answer.authorDates: American columnist & Baltimore & Ohio Railroad passenger agent, fl. 1911 · wrote the “Stub Ends of Thoughts” column
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Mark Twain (who died in 1910) ever said this. Quote Investigator traces the earliest instance to columnist Arthur G. Lewis in the April 1911 Book of the Royal Blue, who wrote “It is not the size of the dog in the fight that counts, but the fight in the dog that wins.” The Twain credit is a modern invention first documented in print in 1991.

source.trailTitle: How the saying is actually sourced
trail: Quote Investigator found the earliest match in the April 1911 Book of the Royal Blue, where columnist Arthur G. Lewis wrote “It is not the size of the dog in the fight that counts, but the fight in the dog that wins.”
The Center for Mark Twain Studies confirms the line is apocryphal, noting Twain died in 1910 — before the saying is first recorded — and was an unlikely champion of dog-fighting imagery.

President Dwight D. Eisenhower gave the adage a boost in a 31 January 1958 speech — “What counts is not necessarily the size of the dog in the fight—it’s the size of the fight in the dog” — long after it had entered common speech, per Quote Investigator.
source.excerptNote: Arthur G. Lewis’s original 1911 wording. The now-familiar “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight, it’s the size of the fight in the dog” is a later, smoothed-out paraphrase that evolved over the following decades.

source.rightsNote: The earliest documented form appeared in a 1911 American periodical, placing the saying’s origin well before 1931 and in the public domain. Note that the exact modern wording is a folk paraphrase that evolved anonymously over decades rather than a fixed phrase from a single copyrighted work.

author.name: Arthur G. Lewis
author.heading: Who was Arthur G. Lewis?
author.metaLine: fl. 1911 · American columnist & railroad passenger agent
author.bio: Arthur G. Lewis was a little-known American writer who penned an aphoristic feature called Stub Ends of Thoughts. His epigram about the fighting spirit of a small dog appeared in the April 1911 issue of the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad’s passenger magazine, Book of the Royal Blue. From that modest column the saying spread anonymously for a century, evolving into the polished modern proverb and eventually being misattributed to far more famous names.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “famous name” misattribution: a punchy proverb of unknown authorship gets welded onto a beloved wit. Mark Twain is the leading magnet, but he is far from the only one credited.

items.why: Twain died in April 1910 — a year before the saying’s first known appearance. Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence he used it, and the Center for Mark Twain Studies lists it among his apocryphal quotations.
Eisenhower did use a version in a 31 January 1958 speech, which is why his name attaches to it — but the saying was already decades old by then, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented author is columnist Arthur G. Lewis, in the April 1911 Book of the Royal Blue, as established by Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The saying survives because it is a perfect piece of folk wisdom: a compact chiasmus (“size of the dog in the fight / size of the fight in the dog”) that flips a memorable image into an inspirational point about grit over stature. Lines like this rarely stay anonymous — they drift toward whichever famous wit feels plausible.

Mark Twain is the internet’s single biggest destination for orphaned aphorisms, so once the credit surfaced in print — a 1991 newspaper, then a 1997 public-speaking handbook — it stuck and multiplied. The irony, as Twain scholars note, is that Twain — an outspoken friend to animals — is an especially poor fit for a metaphor rooted in dog-fighting.
context.pull: Twain died in 1910 — a year before the saying was first written down.
